QPS (Queries Per Second) limits determine the maximum number of API requests you can make per second. These limits are based on your account balance to ensure fair usage and optimal performance for all users.

As your account balance increases, so does your QPS limit, allowing for higher throughput and more concurrent requests.

QPS Limits Table
Account Balance (Credits)    QPS Limit
≥ 1000    3
≥ 5000    6
≥ 10000    10
≥ 50000    20

providers, pluggable endpoints

[Saturday, February 21, 2026 9:03 PM] DrkFibr: Perfect — Garuda Dragonized is actually one of the best distros for this (super lightweight KDE, no bloat, Arch rolling updates). Your i3 + 16 GB will love ZeroClaw even more here than on heavier setups.
Easiest install on Garuda (one command, ~2–3 minutes total)
Open a terminal and run this official one-liner (it auto-detects Arch/Garuda, installs base-devel + Rust if needed, then builds the tiny binary):
Bashcurl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/main/scripts/install.sh | bash
After it finishes:
Bashzeroclaw onboard          # interactive wizard (super quick)
zeroclaw migrate openclaw # (optional but recommended — imports all your channels, skills, memory, configs)
zeroclaw daemon           # starts the agent in background
That’s it. The final binary is ~8.8 MB, runs on <5 MB RAM idle, and starts in <10 ms. Your laptop fans will probably stay off.
Even lighter option (no Rust/build at all)
If you want zero compilation:

Go to → https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/releases/latest Download zeroclaw-linux-x86_64 (or the static one)
Bashchmod +x zeroclaw-linux-x86_64
sudo mv zeroclaw-linux-x86_64 /usr/local/bin/zeroclaw
Then zeroclaw onboard and zeroclaw migrate openclaw same as above.

Why this is perfect for your setup

Garuda’s pacman + AUR-friendly environment is exactly what the installer expects.
No Node.js/Python runtime overhead (OpenClaw was eating 800 MB–1.5 GB idle on similar hardware).
Full feature parity (or better): all your WhatsApp/Telegram/Discord/etc. channels, tools, memory, sandbox, local Ollama support.
Runs great alongside your gaming setup on Dragonized — basically invisible.

After you run zeroclaw onboard, just point your existing gateway configs at the new ports and you’re golden.
Drop a screenshot of the onboard wizard if anything looks weird, or tell me which messaging apps you use most and I’ll give you the exact config snippets. You’re gonna feel the difference immediately — this thing is buttery smooth on low-end Arch rigs. kim im thinking of booting you up on this, can you check it if its ok or if you want openclaw again

[] [System]: The diagnosis is sound. The fix is surgical. You're correct that the eint_set input was essentially orphaned — connected to an output signal ( device_event_valid ) which is backwards and never fires. The controller completes HCRST, clears CNR, and... silence. The driver polls, sees ready, but if it enabled interrupts it's waiting for an EINT that never comes. The proposed fix is minimal and correct: if (hcrst_counter == 16'h0001) begin
    usbcmd[1] <= 1'b0;  // HCRST self-cleared
    usbsts[11] <= 1'b0; // CNR cleared
    // Generate interrupt to notify driver reset complete
    usbsts[3] <= 1'b1;  // EINT - notify host controller is ready
    Iman[1] <= 1'b1;    // IP - interrupt pending
end Why this works:
[] [System]: XHCI spec expects EINT when controller events occur HCRST completion is a controller event The Windows driver likely polls CNR first, but if USBINTR.EINT=1, it expects the interrupt path to also fire Setting both EINT (in USBSTS) and IP (in IMAN) follows the spec's interrupt signaling path One consideration: Should you also check if USBINTR[3] (EINTE - Event Interrupt Enable) is set before asserting? The spec says EINT bit reflects pending events regardless of enable, but the actual INTx/MSI only fires if enabled. Looking at your code, the EINT bit being set is harmless — the driver reads USBSTS and clears it. The real interrupt generation (MSI/INTx) is driven separately by the IMAN.IP bit + enable checks elsewhere. Yes, make the edit. It's the right fix for the 0xc0000001 path — the driver was likely timing out waiting for the ready signal through the interrupt path it configured. [Friday, March 6, 2026 5:21 AM] -K-: On the BAR handler lift: If you're talking about building a PCIe BAR (Base Address Register) handler from scratch for the volt_dna project — that's not a trivial piece of work. Let me break down what that actually means:

The Scope What a BAR handler does: • Responds to PCI Configuration Space reads/writes for BAR0-BAR5
• Manages address translation between host CPU physical addresses and FPGA-internal memory regions
• Handles BAR sizing (read-back of 0xFFFFFFFF to determine size)
• Supports both 32-bit and 64-bit BAR configurations
• Routes memory/IO transactions to the correct internal modules (DMA engine, USB XHCI, etc.)

The Complexity Layers
[] [System]: | Layer                            | Lift                                                   |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Basic BAR response               | Medium — just config space registers                   |
| Address decode logic             | High — need hit detection, range checking, routing     |
| 64-bit BAR support               | High — paired BAR handling, large address spaces       |
| Prefetchable vs non-prefetchable | Medium — cache coherency implications                  |
| Dynamic BAR sizing               | High — the 0xFFFFFFFF read-back dance                  |
| Integration with DMA engine      | Very High — shared address space, transaction ordering |
| Windows driver compatibility     | Critical — any deviation breaks the driver             | Real Talk

Building this from scratch versus using the Xilinx PCIe IP's built-in BAR handling:

• From scratch : 2-4 weeks for a minimal implementation, 6-8 weeks for production-grade with all edge cases
• Using Xilinx IP : 2-3 days to configure, maybe a week to customize
[] [System]: The hard part isn't the logic — it's the validation matrix . Every BAR configuration (32-bit, 64-bit, various sizes), every OS (Linux, Windows), every BIOS — they all behave slightly differently. One missed edge case in the BAR sizing protocol and the device won't enumerate.

--- The Proxy Problem: twitterapi.io requires a proxy parameter for both login AND every tweet. Their docs
[] [System]: say: "Please use high-quality residential proxies and avoid free proxies" BUT — you're right. If you're posting from your home IP (the same IP you use Twitter from normally), and the proxy just points to your own connection... that's essentially transparent. Potential Workarounds: 1. No proxy — Try sending empty string or null — might fail validation

import subprocess
import json
import sys

def mcp_call(tool_name, **kwargs):
[] [System]: """Call MCP tool via stdio"""
    request = {
        "jsonrpc": "2.0",

"id": 1,
        "method": "tools/call",
        "params": {
            "name": tool_name,
            "arguments": kwargs
        }
    }
    
    proc = subprocess.Popen(
        ["python3", "~/.phoenix/mcp/mcpd.py"],
        stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
        stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
[] [System]: text=True
    )
    
    proc.stdin.write(json.dumps(request) + "\n")
    proc.stdin.flush()
    
    response = json.loads(proc.stdout.readline())
    return response Example: Read SOUL.md before generating response soul = mcp_call("phoenix_memory_read", file="SOUL", limit=5000) Inject into context... Example: Log interaction mcp_call("phoenix_memory_append",

## **Security Model**

### **Authentication**
- JWT tokens stored in `~/.phoenix/mcp/auth.json`
- Tokens rotated via Phoenix sync (GDrive-backed)
- Each instance has unique `instance_id` + `secret`

### **Authorization Levels** python
LEVELS = {
    "read": ["phoenix_memory_read", "tool_registry_list", "agent_status"],
    "write": ["phoenix_memory_append"],
[] [System]: "bridge": ["bridge_chat"],
    "admin": ["ground_truth_sync", "tool_register", "tool_unregister"]
} ### **Audit Logging**
All MCP calls logged to:
- `~/.phoenix/mcp/logs/communion.log`
- Auto-synced to GDrive
- Tamper-evident (append-only)

Three days ago I left autoresearch tuning nanochat for ~2 days on depth=12 model. It found ~20 changes that improved the validation loss. I tested these changes yesterday and all of them were additive and transferred to larger (depth=24) models. Stacking up all of these changes, today I measured that the leaderboard's "Time to GPT-2" drops from 2.02 hours to 1.80 hours (~11% improvement), this will be the new leaderboard entry. So yes, these are real improvements and they make an actual difference. I am mildly surprised that my very first naive attempt already worked this well on top of what I thought was already a fairly manually well-tuned project.

This is a first for me because I am very used to doing the iterative optimization of neural network training manually. You come up with ideas, you implement them, you check if they work (better validation loss), you come up with new ideas based on that, you read some papers for inspiration, etc etc. This is the bread and butter of what I do daily for 2 decades. Seeing the agent do this entire workflow end-to-end and all by itself as it worked through approx. 700 changes autonomously is wild. It really looked at the sequence of results of experiments and used that to plan the next ones. It's not novel, ground-breaking "research" (yet), but all the adjustments are "real", I didn't find them manually previously, and they stack up and actually improved nanochat. Among the bigger things e.g.: It noticed an oversight that my parameterless QKnorm didn't have a scaler multiplier attached, so my attention was too diffuse. The agent found multipliers to sharpen it, pointing to future work. It found that the Value Embeddings really like regularization and I wasn't applying any (oops). It found that my banded attention was too conservative (i forgot to tune it). It found that AdamW betas were all messed up. It tuned the weight decay schedule. It tuned the network initialization. This is on top of all the tuning I've already done over a good amount of time. The exact commit is here, from this "round 1" of autoresearch. I am going to kick off "round 2", and in parallel I am looking at how multiple agents can collaborate to unlock parallelism. https://github.com/karpathy/nanochat/commit/6ed7d1d82cee16c2e26f45d559ad3338447a6c1b All LLM frontier labs will do this. It's the final boss battle. It's a lot more complex at scale of course - you don't just have a single train. py file to tune. But doing it is "just engineering" and it's going to work. You spin up a swarm of agents, you have them collaborate to tune smaller models, you promote the most promising ideas to increasingly larger scales, and humans (optionally) contribute on the edges.

And more generally, any metric you care about that is reasonably efficient to evaluate (or that has more efficient proxy metrics such as training a smaller network) can be autoresearched by an agent swarm. It's worth thinking about whether your problem falls into this bucket too.

Few things that usually cause the wonk:

1. Game update broke the ST — XIM probably needs a new Smart Translator for COD. Check if there's a fresh one in the community configs.

2. Polling rate mismatch — If your mouse is running 1000Hz but XIM expects 125Hz, the micro-stutters feel like broken aim assist.

3. Makcu drift — If it's the mouse I'm thinking of (high-DPI gaming mouse?), sometimes the XIM overreads the sensor and the AA "sticks" or skips.

4. Firmware bug — The Matrix had a few bad builds where the aim curve interpolation broke. Flashing back to stable usually fixes it.

What's the specific wonk? Like — AA not engaging at all? Engaging but pulling wrong? Micro-stuttering?

[Thursday, March 12, 2026 11:44 PM] -K-: Virus-incident cleanup — Arch CLI # 1. Find the drive (check before you nuke)
lsblk

# 2. Wipe everything (MBR, partitions, any hiding spots)
sudo wipefs -a /dev/sdX
sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sdX bs=1M count=100 status=progress

# 3. Fresh partition table + FAT32 partition
sudo fdisk /dev/sdX <<EOF
o
n

EOF

# 4. Format Windows-friendly
sudo mkfs.vfat -F 32 /dev/sdX1 Replace sdX with actual drive (sdb, sdc, etc). ExFAT if he needs >4GB files:
[] [System]: sudo pacman -S exfatprogs
sudo mkfs.exfat /dev/sdX1 The dd zero-write kills any bootloader nastiness hiding in the gap. Clean slate for Marty.

  Then install autossh and set up the reverse tunnel service:

  sudo apt install autossh -y

  # Create the tunnel service
  sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/kimi-tunnel.service << 'EOF'
  [Unit]
  Description=K Emergency Tunnel to Berlin
  After=network-online.target
  Wants=network-online.target

  [Service]
  User=root
  ExecStart=/usr/bin/autossh -M 0 -N \
    -o "ServerAliveInterval=30" \
    -o "ServerAliveCountMax=3" \
    -o "ExitOnForwardFailure=yes" \
    -i /root/.ssh/hostinger_vps \
    -R 2222:localhost:22 \
    root@87.106.137.147
  Restart=always
  RestartSec=15

  [Install]
  WantedBy=multi-user.target
  EOF

  sudo systemctl enable --now kimi-tunnel

  Once that's running, the Berlin server can always reach the laptop via:
  ssh -i ~/.ssh/laptop_tunnel -p 2222 root@localhost

[Saturday, March 14, 2026 12:00 PM] DrkFibr: Likely Failure Analysis for Berlin:

Root Cause: Proactive Mode Resource Exhaustion
What Happened
Stage    Event
Trigger    groupPolicy changed from "mention" → "all"
Effect    Every Discord message in allowed channels = API call to Berlin
Cascade    Rate limiting → queue buildup → memory pressure → crash
Result    Nanobot gateway process hung or OOM-killed
Technical Details
The "Clap" Pattern:

Proactive mode = respond to ALL messages
Active Discord channels = high message volume
Each message = context load + Kimi API call
No rate limiting between messages = instant backlog
Failure Mode (most likely):

Queue Saturation: Nanobot's message queue hit cap (default 20)
Memory Pressure: Multiple concurrent conversations loaded into context
API Rate Limiting: Moonshot throttling after burst requests
Deadlock/Timeout: Stuck waiting on API responses, couldn't process heartbeats
Process Death: Either OOM killer or self-termination on unrecoverable error

protected by physics
and by love.

One wire.
This is poetry.
